newsitem.title: GERMANY: Leica says slow deliveries hit 96/97 profit.
newsitem.headline: Leica says slow deliveries hit 96/97 profit.

text.p: Germany's Leica Camera AG on Monday reported a 7.4 percent drop in operating earnings in its 1996/1997 business year as returns were hampered by delayed deliveries of new products and a slowdown in demand for compact cameras.

But the Swiss-owned manufacturer of prestige cameras, reporting preliminary results for the year to March 31, 1997, said it had nonetheless achieved its sales target for the year with a 10.7 percent rise in turnover to 265.6 million marks ($159.2 million).
Teething problems with new products would be ironed out in the current year, Leica said, so that the new camera and lens models should make their positive impact on margins felt soon.
"Leica expects double-digit sales growth in the current business year and good results," the Solms, Germany, based company said in a statement.
Operating profit for the 1996/1997 year fell to 15.2 million marks while gross earnings were slightly above year-ago levels at 69.2 million marks.

The news put pressure on the newly-listed company's shares, which dropped more than seven percent to a record low of 46.50 marks in early bourse trade, below their price at issue last September of 47 marks.

The delivery delays were caused by unexpected production difficulties, which meant just 5,000 of Leica's new R8 manual focus cameras were delivered in the year. Production plans for the R8 are for 1,000 units a month.
In addition, Leica said only around a third of a range of new lens models which it launched successfully at the giant Photokina camera trade fair in Cologne last year had been delivered to customers.
The camera maker said it had introduced measures to speed up its own operations and those of third parties and was confident of significantly improving the delivery situation in the months to come.

Delay had not meant a slowdown in customer orders, Leica said, with orders in hand for R8s, priced at 4,400 marks excluding the lens, stood at more than 3,000 units, the highest ever seen for a new model.
The tough market for compact cameras, especially in Germany, sent sales in that segment down 25 percent to 32.4 million marks, Leica said.
Leica, a favourite among photography purists, said it would have to focus more on differentiating itself from the herd and focus on the top end of the compact market.

Minox, Leica's new compact camera unit, did not manage to break even as had been planned in the fourth quarter, but Leica said its products had been well received and that the unit should more than double its sales and turn to profit this year.
Breaking down its performance this year, Leica said its German shares fell six percent to 94.8 million marks, while European sales outside Germany rose three percent to 68.4 million marks.
Asian and Australian sales rose 41 percent to 63.2 million marks, while U.S. sales advanced 47 percent to 34.8 million marks. ($ = 1.668 German Marks)
